claims.text: Targeted thermomechanical treatment that induces phase-selective recrystallization will simultaneously increase strength and ductility relative to conventional processing.
The eutectic high-entropy alloy has duplex soft and hard phases.
Both phases in the initial alloy are as-cast or conventionally processed.
Conventionally processed eutectic alloys have limited ductility.
The limited ductility results from weak phase boundaries and insufficient strain partitioning.
A tailored combination of annealing and deformation can trigger recrystallization selectively in the soft phase.
The intervention retains the hard-phase skeleton while recrystallizing the soft phase.
The soft phase must recrystallize completely without significant alteration of hard-phase morphology.
A controlled temperature and deformation rate promote phase-selective recrystallization.
The resulting microstructure consists of a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in a hard-phase skeleton.
The hard-phase skeleton remains minimally changed by the treatment.
Selective recrystallization enhances ductility by eliminating weak boundaries.
The retained hard-phase skeleton maintains high strength.
Manipulating strain partitioning between the two phases releases or maximizes the alloy's strain-hardening capacity.
The treated alloy can achieve approximately 35% uniform elongation.
The treated alloy can reach approximately 2 GPa true stress.
The treated alloy will retain or improve ultimate strength relative to the conventional baseline.
Conventionally processed baseline alloys undergo premature cracking at weak phase boundaries.
Over-recrystallization or complete microstructural homogenization may negate the mechanical benefit.
Process sensitivity to parameters and composition, and scalability to industrial production, remain uncertain.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis and falsification rule require an increase in strength, whereas the predicted outcome allows strength merely to be retained. Thus, a ductility increase with unchanged strength would satisfy the predicted outcome but falsify the headline hypothesis and stated rule.
